title: Twenty-four conditions
hookLine: the great book of relations: how things condition each other in twenty-four ways

cards: The commentaries tell a story about a book. After his awakening, they say, the Buddha spent days reflecting on the teachings that would become the Abhidhamma, one after another, and nothing unusual happened.
Then he came to the last of them, a vast teaching about how things relate. And as his mind moved through it, rays of light in six colors streamed from his body.
The commentators' point is plain: this one had room enough for a mind like his.

teach.b: The book is the Patthana, the book of relations, which the tradition places last in the Abhidhamma basket and calls the great treatise.
For days this path has been taking things apart: mind into moments, moments into factors, matter into elements. The Patthana puts them back together. Its question isn't what is there.
It's how each thing leans on the others.
It names twenty-four ways one thing can condition another. Some sound familiar.
Root: greed or kindness holding a moment up from below. Object: the thing the mind takes up. Nutriment: food for the body, and contact and intention as food for the mind.
Kamma: an intention now conditioning a result later. Some sound stranger. Presence: something helps just by being there.
Absence: something helps by having just gone, the way one mind-moment makes room for the next by vanishing. Then the book works them through, combination after combination, at great length.
What's it for on an ordinary day?

teach.h: NOT ONE CAUSE, BUT A WEB.
teach.b: It breaks the habit of one cause. When a friend snaps at you, the easy story is a single reason: they're rude, or you did something wrong.
The Patthana's picture is a web: their tiredness, an old memory, the tone of your message, an empty stomach, the weather, a root of irritation, a moment of attention missing.
None of it is the whole cause, and nothing stands outside the web. Back on day four hundred thirty-four, a whole life was traced by conditions.
The suttas say it in a few words: when this is, that is; when this arises, that arises. The Patthana spends a whole book showing how.

how: In Theravada communities, monks and lay students study the Patthana, and Abhidhamma courses teach its conditions as a way of seeing how things depend on each other.

games.q: a friend snaps at you out of nowhere. you want to know why. what picture does the Patthana offer?
o: a web of conditions leaning on each other
no reason at all: it just happened
games.why: a web: tiredness, memory, tone, hunger, a root of irritation. none of it is the whole cause, and nothing stands outside the web.

practice: Pick one thing you can feel right now, the ease in your shoulders or the tightness, and ask gently what's holding it up: the chair, last night's sleep, something someone said this morning.
Don't solve it; let two or three conditions show themselves, and notice that each of them leans on others too. Then come back to the breath, which is leaning on air.
